claims.text: Increasing solvent viscosity during low-temperature colloidal synthesis restricts precursor mobility.
Restricted precursor or atom mobility favors kinetic trapping of a homogeneous, single-phase noble-metal high-entropy alloy.
The resulting single-phase alloy contains highly isolated noble-metal sites.
A homogeneous single-phase structure with isolated noble-metal sites leads to improved catalytic performance.
A high-molecular-weight stabilizer can be used to increase solvent viscosity in the proposed colloidal synthesis.
Low-temperature synthesis at 80–120 °C under an inert atmosphere is an appropriate regime for the proposed viscosity comparison.
Higher solvent viscosity reduces atomic diffusion during nucleation.
Limited mobility opposes element-specific mixing preferences and reduces microsegregation.
Alloy formation in a limited-mobility five-element system follows stochastic principles that favor a random alloy.
High-viscosity synthesis will produce a narrower nanoparticle size distribution than the low-viscosity baseline.
High-viscosity synthesis will produce more uniform elemental and site dispersion than the low-viscosity baseline.
High-viscosity synthesis will yield higher catalytic turnover than the low-viscosity baseline.
High-viscosity synthesis will lower the activation energy of nitrobenzene hydrogenation relative to the baseline.
The hypothesis should hold in low-temperature regimes dominated by diffusion-limited kinetics.
The hypothesis may cease to hold at extreme viscosity or where thermal diffusion and mixing are governed by other factors.
There is an optimal viscosity range that improves alloy homogeneity without impairing mass transfer or reduction kinetics.
The magnitude of the catalytic effect may vary with reaction type and synthesis scale.
Failure to obtain statistically significant improvements in both alloy homogeneity and catalytic performance would falsify the proposed governing role of restricted precursor mobility.

contradictions.description: The comparison is described as varying only solvent viscosity, but viscosity is changed by adding a high-molecular-weight stabilizer only to the treatment. Stabilizer presence and its possible chemical or surface effects therefore also differ between treatment and baseline.
